body:
Kleftiko is one of those places where the boat is not just transport.

It is part of the experience.

The white volcanic cliffs, sea arches, caves and strange rock formations sit on the southwest coast of Milos, far from the island’s main roads.

Most visitors who see Kleftiko properly arrive from the sea.

The confusing part comes before you leave the harbour.

**Sailboat or speedboat?**

Both can take you to Kleftiko.

But they create two very different days.

## Short answer

Choose a **sailboat** if you want a slower, more relaxed day at sea, more deck space, lunch on board and time to enjoy the journey itself.

Choose a **speedboat** if you want to reach Kleftiko faster, fit more places into a shorter trip, or combine it with remote stops such as Polyaigos.

Neither is automatically better.

The right choice depends mostly on how much time you have, how you feel about long boat days and what the weather allows.

## Why Kleftiko is worth doing by boat

Kleftiko is not a normal beach.

It is a landscape of pale volcanic rock rising directly from the sea, broken into arches, narrow passages and sheltered coves.

Visit Greece describes it as a collection of huge grey-white rocks surrounded by labyrinthine caves and protected anchorages.

From land, you can reach the wider area only by a demanding hike.

From the sea, the geography suddenly makes sense.

You swim between the formations.

You see the caves from water level.

And in calm conditions, small boats or tenders can take you closer to passages that the larger sailing boats cannot enter.

That is why the boat trip matters here.

[Compare private boat options in Milos](https://click-and-boat.pxf.io/enGWGX "affiliate-button")

## What the sailboat experience is really like

A typical sailing day around Milos is not really about getting somewhere quickly.

It is about spending the day at sea.

Many full-day trips last roughly eight to ten hours and include several swimming stops, food, drinks and time at Kleftiko.

Some itineraries also continue toward Polyaigos, depending on the route and weather.

Recent traveller reviews repeatedly praise the relaxed pace, homemade-style food, small groups and crews that make the day feel personal rather than rushed.

One thing worth understanding, though:

The word **“sailing”** does not guarantee that you will spend the whole day silently moving under sail.

Depending on wind, route and timing, the engine may be used for significant parts of the trip.

That does not necessarily make the trip worse.

It just means you should book a sailboat because you like the style of the day, not because you expect a romantic sailing movie for ten straight hours.

## What the speedboat experience is really like

A speedboat changes the equation.

Travel time becomes shorter.

That means operators can fit several distant places into a half-day or full-day itinerary.

Kleftiko.

Sykia.

Gerakas.

Sometimes Polyaigos.

Sometimes even parts of the north or east coast if conditions allow.

This is the big attraction.

You spend less of the day travelling slowly between stops and more time jumping between places.

Small RIB-style boats can also approach narrow coastal formations more easily than a large sailing yacht or catamaran.

But there is a trade-off.

The ride itself can be much more physical.

If the sea is rough, a fast boat bouncing across chop is very different from sitting on the deck of a larger vessel.

That matters if you have back problems, dislike rough rides or simply want a lazy day.

## Sailboat or speedboat?

### Choose a sailboat if you want…

* a slower, more relaxed day at sea
* more room to sit, move around and stay in the shade
* a proper onboard lunch rather than just snacks
* fewer stops, but more time at each one
* the journey itself to feel like part of the holiday

For couples, slower travellers and anyone who wants a full-day experience, this is usually the more enjoyable option.

### Choose a speedboat if you want…

* to reach Kleftiko faster
* to fit more places into half a day
* a better chance of combining Kleftiko with Sykia or Polyaigos
* more swimming and exploring, less time simply sitting on deck
* a shorter, more active day

The trade-off is comfort: smaller fast boats can feel much rougher when the sea is choppy.

### My simple rule

**Sailboat = the better day at sea.**

**Speedboat = the better way to cover more places quickly.**

Neither is automatically better.

The real question is what kind of day you want.

## The part people underestimate: the wind

The Cyclades are windy.

In summer, the Meltemi can become strong enough to change a boat trip completely.

This is not a minor detail buried in the terms and conditions.

Operators sometimes change the departure port, reverse the route, move entirely to the south coast or remove Polyaigos from the itinerary.

Recent traveller reports describe exactly this happening.

One full-day sailing group had its departure moved because of strong northerly winds and spent the day along the protected south coast instead of completing the expected route.

Another traveller booked specifically for Polyaigos but could not visit it because of weather.

Neither case means the operator did anything wrong.

It means Milos is an island and the sea gets the final vote.

## Does that mean speedboats are better in wind?

Not automatically.

This is where marketing claims become dangerous.

A speedboat is faster and more flexible.

But fast does not mean comfortable in rough water.

A larger catamaran or sailing vessel may feel steadier, while a small RIB can become a very lively ride.

The skipper and the route matter more than a simple rule such as “speedboat = better in wind”.

If you are sensitive to motion, ask the operator what happens when the Meltemi is strong.

That answer tells you more than the word written on the side of the boat.

## What recent travellers seem to care about most

After reading recent reviews and discussions, something interesting appears.

People talk surprisingly little about the technical type of boat after the trip.

They talk about:

**the crew**

**how crowded the boat felt**

**how much time they had at Kleftiko**

**the food**

**whether the route changed**

**how rough the sea was**

**whether they reached Polyaigos**

That is useful.

It means choosing the right operator and itinerary may matter more than obsessing over sailboat versus speedboat.

One highly rated sailing trip currently has more than 200 TripAdvisor reviews and a 5.0 rating, with travellers repeatedly mentioning crew hospitality, food and Kleftiko.

A popular half-day speedboat option also receives very strong reviews, particularly for its swim stops, crew and ability to cover the route efficiently.

The boats are different.

The things people remember are remarkably similar.

## The number I would check before booking

Ask how long you actually spend at Kleftiko.

Not how long the whole tour lasts.

A ten-hour cruise can sound impressive, but if much of that time is travelling between distant points, it may not give you dramatically more time at Kleftiko than a shorter route.

Likewise, a half-day trip may be perfect if Kleftiko is your only real priority.

Look for the actual stop duration.

That is much more useful than the words “full-day adventure”.

## What about Polyaigos?

This changes the decision.

Polyaigos is an uninhabited island east of Milos known for extraordinarily clear blue water.

If seeing both **Kleftiko and Polyaigos** is important to you, check the itinerary very carefully.

Some full-day sailing tours include both.

Speedboats can combine them more easily because they cover the distance faster.

But Polyaigos is also one of the first things that can disappear from an itinerary when weather conditions are wrong.

So never choose a tour solely because Polyaigos appears in the headline.

Read the weather-change policy.

## I would choose a sailboat if...

You have a full day available.

You enjoy simply being on the sea.

You want space to relax.

Lunch and drinks on board matter to you.

You are travelling as a couple or want a calmer atmosphere.

You would rather have fewer stops and enjoy them properly.

For me, this feels like the more “Greek island day” version of the experience.

The boat ride itself becomes part of the holiday.

## I would choose a speedboat if...

You only want to spend half a day at sea.

You want to cover several places efficiently.

You are especially interested in combining Kleftiko with Polyaigos or other remote coves.

You prefer swimming and exploring to sitting on deck.

You do not mind a potentially bumpier ride if the sea is lively.

This is the version for someone thinking:

**“Show me as much of Milos as possible.”**

## What I would check before paying

Before booking either type, I would verify these things:

### How many passengers?

“Small group” can mean very different things.

Twelve people feels very different from thirty.

### How long at Kleftiko?

This matters more than the total tour duration.

### Is cave access included?

Large vessels normally anchor outside the narrow formations.

Some operators use a tender or small inflatable boat to take guests closer to the caves.

Others expect you to swim.

If this matters to you, ask.

### What happens in strong wind?

Can the departure point change?

Can Polyaigos disappear from the route?

Can you move your booking to another day?

### Is food actually lunch?

Some trips provide a substantial meal.

Others provide snacks.

Neither is wrong.

Just know what you are buying.

### Is there shade?

This becomes surprisingly important after several hours under the Cycladic sun.

Especially on smaller speedboats.

## One thing I would not do

I would not choose purely by price.

The difference between two tours may represent:

a smaller group,

more shade,

a proper meal,

a longer Kleftiko stop,

a better boat,

or simply a more expensive operator.

Look at what actually changes before deciding that one option is overpriced.

## Dan’s take

I have not taken these specific Milos tours myself.

I went through current itineraries, operator information, recent traveller reviews and discussions because this is exactly the kind of choice I would get stuck on before a trip.

And I think I would choose differently depending on the day.

For my first visit to Milos, with no rush?

**Small-group sailboat.**

I like the idea that Kleftiko is not something I race toward, photograph and leave.

I would want the sea, lunch, swimming and the slow approach to be part of the memory.

But if I only had four or five hours — or if seeing Polyaigos mattered more to me than lounging on deck — I would take the speedboat.

That is probably the real answer.

Do not ask which boat is better.

Ask what kind of day you want.

## Before you book

Routes around Milos can change because of wind and sea conditions, even after you have booked.

Check the current itinerary, maximum group size, cancellation terms and whether Kleftiko and Polyaigos are guaranteed stops or weather-dependent.

And if the forecast looks rough, ask the operator what they expect the day to look like.

A good answer from the skipper is worth more than a hundred perfect Instagram photos.
